Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
In article <1183042506.9...@n60g2000hse.googlegroups.com>,
jak...@gmail.com wrote:

> I like my version better. Deals with Rush, deals with votes and deals
> with bleeds more reliably.

Which one? The Helena (?) one? Yeah, probably deals with most threats
better, but doesn't get going for a while, and can't declare attempt to
withdraw till it is probably too late--you have to get out a 10 cap
first (3 turns minimum), and then get rid of the deck. By which time,
your predator and/or prey can probably prevent the withdrawl pretty
easily.

The March Halcyon trick works 'cause you always can act on your second
turn and it is unlikely that someone will prevent you from depleting
your deck on T2 (unless, say, your predator influences out like, David
Morgan, the Scourge who uses his inherrent +1 intercept to block March
and then Undead Strengths her into torpor...). So you can attempt to
withdraw on T3 and only have to deal with the threats available to your
predator (and maybe prey) on T3, which usually isn't *that* much. With
the big vampire deck, you have to try and withdraw on, like, T6 or so,
which will be *much* harder.



Can you use Obedience during your withdrawal attempt (and not fail to
withdraw)? The old text made it clear you could - the new text I'm
not so sure about:

Obedience

Only usable when this reacting vampire is about to enter combat with
an acting younger vampire.

dom: Untap the acting vampire, do not tap this reacting vampire, and
end the current action (and combat). The acting vampire cannot attempt
the same action this turn.

Obedience used to 'cancel' the action and never reach combat. Now it
seems to 'end' both the action and combat - which makes it sound like
you've actually been in combat, which, if true, voids withdrawal.

Alex
